title: Safety Culture & Hazard Recognition

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Shop floor in front of the service trucks, morning light. Medium shot.
scenes.says: Welcome to your first lesson. Before you change a single lamp, I want you to hear this from me: nothing we do is worth getting hurt over. Every lighting job mixes three serious hazards: electricity, heights, and people or equipment moving below you. Electrocutions and falls are among the leading causes of death in our kind of work. Most of them come from shortcuts that always worked before.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Kyle walking past a crew loading a van, tracking shot.
scenes.on_screen: Safety culture = what you do when nobody is watching
scenes.says: A safety culture is what people do when nobody is watching. Here, it means we plan the job before we start it. We report near misses so the next person doesn't get hurt. We never assume a circuit is dead. We test it. And production never outranks safety. If the schedule and safety conflict, safety wins, and you call your supervisor.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Close-up on Kyle, direct to camera.
scenes.on_screen: You are not qualified to work on or near exposed energized parts
scenes.says: One rule for you, starting today. As an entry-level technician, you are not qualified to work on or near exposed energized parts. If a task would require it, stop and get your supervisor. No exceptions.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Customer warehouse aisle with high-bay fixtures, before work starts. A senior tech and a new hire stand with a ladder still on its side. Kyle voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: The Hazard Hunt: 2 minutes, top to bottom
scenes.says: Now let's walk a real job. Before you set up a ladder or open a fixture, take two minutes and scan the area, top to bottom. We call it the hazard hunt. Watch our senior tech do it out loud.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Senior tech points up at a fixture with a cracked lens next to sprinkler pipe, then down at a wet floor and a forklift aisle, then at a ladder with a missing foot. Presenter voice-over; quick cuts on each hazard.
scenes.on_screen: 1. Overhead  2. At the fixture  3. Working height  4. Floor  5. Surroundings  6. People
scenes.says: Overhead: pipes, ductwork, cable trays, open junction boxes. At the fixture: a cracked lens, burn marks, a burning smell, dangling wires. Working height: is this ladder right for the job? That one's missing a foot, so it's tagged out. Floor: level, dry, solid? Here it's wet, and there's a forklift aisle. Surroundings: is the panel reachable? That one's open. And people: who needs to know the lights are going off?

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Crew of three in a tight circle by the van for a pre-task huddle, clipboard with the pre-task plan. Kyle voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Pre-task plan: Steps? What can go wrong? Controls? Who do we call?
scenes.says: Then the crew does the pre-task plan, also called a job hazard analysis. It's short. What are the steps? What can go wrong at each step? What will we do to prevent it? And who do we call, and where do we go, if someone gets hurt? Fill it out honestly, and update it when anything changes.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Kyle in front of a whiteboard with an inverted pyramid drawn on it, medium shot.
scenes.says: When we fix a hazard, we start at the top of the hierarchy of controls. Eliminate it, like de-energizing the circuit. Substitute something safer, like a lift instead of a tall ladder. Use engineering controls like barriers and covers. Then procedures and training. PPE is last. It's the last line of defense, not the first. That's why lockout/tagout is the foundation of what we do.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.background: Back in the warehouse aisle. A tech starts to climb; another tech raises a hand. Kyle voice-over, then cut to Kyle on camera.
scenes.says: Every person here has the authority and the duty to stop work, from your first day. An unexpected voltage reading. A damaged ladder or meter. Someone without their PPE. Anything that makes you uneasy. Say it calmly: Stop, I have a safety concern. Make the area safe if you can, explain what you saw, call your supervisor. For safety, you don't need anyone's permission. Nobody gets disciplined for a good-faith stop. Calling a job for efficiency or quality is different: get your manager's buy-off first.

scenes.speaker: Kyle McClelland
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: So: scan top to bottom before every task. Plan the job. De-energizing beats PPE every time. And if something's wrong, stop the work. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Senior tech performs the hazard hunt on camera; Kyle narrates scenes 4-6 and 8 as voice-over. Staged hazards: open panel (cover removed by a qualified person, area kept clear, nobody approaches), wet floor without a sign, marked forklift aisle, cracked lens, ladder with a missing foot carrying a DO NOT USE tag. Pre-task plan form as a prop. No customer logos in the warehouse.
